title: The Response of Juveniles Dichrostachys cinerea and Terminalia sericea Savanna Plants to Single Cutting Disturbance in the Nylsvley Nature Reserve, South Africa
content: The study investigated the juvenile stages of two savanna woody plant species, Dichrostachys cinerea and Terminalia sericea to single cutting disturbance. Due to challenges in protecting experimental sites from external disturbances in communal land, the research utilized line transects and plot-based sampling methods within the Nylsvley Nature Reserve. Juvenile plants were divided into groups of thirty-five, each subjected to monthly cutting to assess their resprout heights and leaf counts in relation to the cutting season. Findings indicated that both species successfully regrew after cutting regardless of the month, with T. sericea exhibiting greater average resprout heights compared to D. cinerea throughout the monitoring period. Seasonal variations showed that winter cuts yielded taller resprout heights compared to other seasons, while summer cuts resulted in shorter heights and fewer leaves. Specifically, winter-cut plants had more resprouting leaves than those cut in autumn and spring, with a significant difference in size; winter leaves were more than double the size of those from summer. Moreover, lower winter root sugar concentrations in Dichrostachys cinerea and Terminalia sericea indicate seasonal reductions in metabolic activity. Overall, T. sericea had fewer resprouting leaves than D. cinerea when averaged over seasons. The study concluded that winter is the optimal season for cutting these juvenile species to manage bush encroachment effectively, while summer is the least effective. This information is crucial for developing management plans aimed at preserving biodiversity, ecological integrity, and the livelihoods dependent on savanna ecosystems.
